newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: The pain of elections grips Africa again.
newsitem.headline: The pain of elections grips Africa again.

text.p: Five years after the fall of Communism inspired democracy campaigners across Africa, the ballot box is turning out to be more than what its champions bargained for.

From Benin to Zambia, elections have left tension, chaos and division in their wake, recalling the heady days of independence in the 1960s which were swiftly followed by military coups and a long era of dictatorship.

Over the past week alone elections have raised tensions in Gabon, Niger, Senegal and Zambia. Authorities in Chad and Gambia have repeatedly postponed legislative elections this year, and both have now set polling for early next year.
Organisational problems have dogged every election in Africa over the past five years, with the exception of South Africa.
But the root of electoral unrest remains what opposition parties see as the manipulation of government institutions and machinery by ruling cliques to hang on to power.

President Frederick Chiluba was re-elected in Zambia's presidential elections last week after his main challenger, former nationalist leader and founding president Kenneth Kaunda, was barred from running.
Kaunda had ruled the Southern African nation for more than a quarter century, but Chiluba's government passed a nationality law which barred Kaunda, a son of immigrants.
A similar law in Ivory Coast seen by the opposition as targeting former Prime Minister Alasane Ouatara was at the root of violence around last year's Ivorian presidential poll.
The trend in West Africa is for army rulers to use state power to launch themselves into politics, legitimising their rule through elections in which opponents stand no chance.

"I lost the elections before they were held. The military denied me the use of state radio and television," lamented third-placed Amath Bah in presidential elections in Gambia last September won by military ruler Yahya Jammeh.

Jammeh, now 31, seized power in a coup in 1994 that ousted elected veteran president Sir Dawda Jawara. Jammeh passed through an electoral law that banned Gambia's main political parties and experienced politicians and then presented himself for election, which he duly won.
Niger's General Ibrahim Bare Mainassara did the same in Niger. After seizing power last January, he won elections in July denounced by the opposition and Western nations as rigged.
The United States suspended aid. Opposition parties demanding a rerun of the presidential vote boycotted legislative elections on Saturday whose turnout was below 30 percent.

A similar scenario played out this year in Chad under General Idriss Deby. Nigerian campaigners are predicting that their own military ruler, General Sani Abacha, would do the same in 1998 when he has promised civilian-rule election.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous country has had little success with elections since independence from Britain in 1960.

Abacha insists he will keep his promise to hand over to a civilian president. But if he decides that he should be the civilian, he has vast resources from Nigeria's oil wealth and powerful state enterprises to use as patronage.

Problems at the organisational level are the ones that are most visible and most likely to trigger violence, as was the case in Gabon last month when voters tired of waiting in line set fire to polling booths during local elections.

A rerun in the capital Libreville on Sunday was plagued by similar problems -- no voter lists or ballot cards, or even polling officials. In local elections in Senegal the same day, voting started late even at the polling station where President Abdou Diouf was registered.
But political analysts say the most important threat to the democratic process in Africa as a whole is control of the rules of the game and the use of patronage.
Manipulation at this level is done long before Western poll monitors arrive to observe the actual voting, they say.

Many Western experts have begun to question the focus on elections as the main route to political change in Africa. There are increasing calls for privatisation as a means of diminishing state power, used by Africa's dictators against their opponents.
